title: Chapter 8 — The Americans Combat Individualism By The Principle Of Interest Rightly Understood
paragraphs: When the world was managed by a few rich and powerful individuals, those people liked to hold a lofty idea of man's duties. They were fond of declaring that it is praiseworthy to forget oneself, and that good should be done without hope of reward, as the Deity himself does it. Such were the standard moral opinions of that age. I doubt that men were more virtuous in aristocratic ages than in others, but they were incessantly talking about the beauty of virtue — its usefulness was studied only in secret. Now that the imagination takes less lofty flights and every man's thoughts are centered on himself, moralists are alarmed by the idea of self-sacrifice and no longer dare to hold it up to the human mind. So they content themselves with asking whether the personal advantage of each member of the community does not consist in working for the good of all. When they hit on some point where private interest and public interest meet and merge, they are quick to point it out. Observations of this kind are gradually multiplied: what was only a single remark becomes a general principle, and it is held as a truth that a man serves himself in serving his fellow creatures, and that his private interest is to do good.

I have already shown, in several parts of this work, by what means the inhabitants of the United States almost always manage to combine their own advantage with that of their fellow citizens. My present purpose is to point out the general rule that allows them to do so. In the United States hardly anyone talks about the beauty of virtue, but they maintain that virtue is useful, and they prove it every day. American moralists do not claim that men ought to sacrifice themselves for their fellow creatures because such sacrifices are noble; they boldly declare that such sacrifices are as necessary to the one who makes them as to the one for whose sake they are made. They have discovered that in their country and their age, man is drawn back to himself by an irresistible force. Giving up all hope of stopping that force, they turn all their thought to directing it. They therefore do not deny that every man may pursue his own interest; rather, they try to prove that it is in every man's interest to be virtuous. I will not go into the reasons they give, which would take me from my subject. It is enough to say that they have convinced their fellow countrymen.

Montaigne said long ago: "If I did not follow the straight road for its straightness, I would follow it for having found by experience that in the end it is usually the happiest and most useful path." The doctrine of interest rightly understood is therefore not new. But among the Americans of our time it meets with universal acceptance. It has become popular there. You can trace it at the bottom of all their actions; you will notice it in everything they say. It is as often found on the lips of the poor man as of the rich. In Europe the principle of interest is much cruder than it is in America, but at the same time it is less common, and especially less openly avowed. Among us, men still constantly pretend to a great self-denial they no longer feel. The Americans, by contrast, are fond of explaining almost every action of their lives by the principle of interest rightly understood. They show with satisfaction how an enlightened concern for themselves constantly prompts them to help each other, and disposes them willingly to sacrifice a share of their time and property to the welfare of the state. In this respect I think they often fail to do themselves justice. For in the United States, as elsewhere, people are sometimes seen giving way to those disinterested and spontaneous impulses that are natural to man. But the Americans rarely admit that they yield to such emotions — they are more anxious to do honor to their philosophy than to themselves.

I might stop here without attempting to pass judgment on what I have described. The extreme difficulty of the subject would excuse me, but I shall not use that excuse. I would rather have my readers, clearly seeing my aim, refuse to follow me, than leave them in suspense. The principle of interest rightly understood is not a lofty one, but it is clear and sure. It does not aim at great objects, but it reaches, without excessive effort, all those it does aim at. Since it lies within the reach of every intelligence, everyone can easily grasp and retain it. Thanks to its admirable fit with human weaknesses, it easily gains great dominion; and that dominion is not precarious, since the principle checks one personal interest by another, using to direct the passions the very instrument that excites them. The principle of interest rightly understood produces no great acts of self-sacrifice, but it suggests daily small acts of self-denial. By itself it cannot make a man virtuous, but it disciplines a great many citizens in habits of regularity, temperance, moderation, foresight, and self-command. If it does not lead men straight to virtue by an act of will, it gradually draws them in that direction through their habits. If the principle of interest rightly understood were to govern the whole moral world, extraordinary virtues would no doubt be rarer; but I think gross depravity would also be less common. The principle perhaps prevents some men from rising far above the level of mankind, but a great many other men, who were falling far below it, are caught and restrained by it. Look at some few individuals — they are lowered by it. Look at mankind as a whole — it is raised. I am not afraid to say that the principle of interest rightly understood seems to me the best suited of all philosophical theories to the needs of the men of our time, and that I regard it as their chief remaining safeguard against themselves. The minds of moralists in our age should therefore turn toward it. Even if they judge it incomplete, it must still be adopted as necessary.

On the whole I do not think there is more selfishness among us than in America. The only difference is that there it is enlightened, and here it is not. Every American will sacrifice a share of his private interests to preserve the rest; we would like to preserve the whole, and often end up losing it all. Everyone around me seems bent on teaching his contemporaries, by precept and example, that what is useful is never wrong. Will no one take on the task of making them understand how what is right may be useful? No power on earth can prevent the growing equality of conditions from inclining the human mind to seek out what is useful, or from leading every member of the community to become wrapped up in himself. We must therefore expect personal interest to become more than ever the chief, if not the only, spring of men's actions. But it remains to be seen how each man will understand his personal interest. If the members of a community, as they grow more equal, also grow more ignorant and coarse, it is hard to foresee to what pitch of stupid excess their selfishness may lead them; and no one can predict into what disgrace and wretchedness they would plunge themselves rather than sacrifice any of their own well-being to the prosperity of their fellow creatures. I do not think that the system of interest as it is professed in America is, in all its parts, self-evident; but it contains a great many truths so evident that men, provided they are educated, cannot fail to see them. Educate, then, at all costs — for the age of implicit self-sacrifice and instinctive virtues is already receding far from us, and the time is fast approaching when freedom, public peace, and social order itself will not be able to exist without education.
